lesson.title: Bitcoin: The Original Blockchain
lesson.summary: Bitcoin, launched in 2009 from a whitepaper by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, was the first blockchain network, built narrowly around peer to peer electronic cash secured by proof of work.
lesson.body:
Bitcoin is the network that introduced the blockchain concept to the world in working form. It was described in a whitepaper published in October 2008 under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, whose real identity has never been publicly and conclusively confirmed, and the network itself went live in January 2009 with the mining of its first block, known as the genesis block. Everything discussed elsewhere in this unit, the chain structure, decentralized consensus, wallets and keys, traces back to this starting point.

Bitcoin's purpose was narrow and deliberate: peer to peer electronic cash, a way for two parties to transfer value directly to each other without relying on a bank or payment processor as a trusted intermediary. That narrowness was a design choice, not a limitation Satoshi failed to notice. By keeping the system focused on payments rather than general computation, Bitcoin's rules stay simple enough to reason about carefully, which matters a great deal for a network meant to secure real value with no central authority able to step in and fix mistakes.

Security in Bitcoin comes from proof of work, the same mechanism referenced earlier when explaining permissionless networks generally. Miners compete to find a value, through repeated computation using the SHA-256 hashing algorithm, that produces a block hash below a target threshold. Whoever finds a valid solution first gets to add the next block and collects the associated reward, and this process is deliberately expensive, since rewriting past history would require redoing that computational work faster than the rest of the honest network combined, which becomes effectively infeasible as more computing power joins the network over time.

Unlike Ethereum, covered in the previous chapter, Bitcoin's scripting language is intentionally limited and not Turing complete. It supports conditions for spending, such as requiring multiple signatures to authorize a transaction, but it was never designed to run arbitrary smart contract logic. This keeps Bitcoin's attack surface and behavior simple and predictable, at the cost of the general programmability that made Ethereum attractive for building broader applications.

Bitcoin also has a fixed, engineered scarcity built directly into its protocol: total supply is capped at 21 million bitcoin, and the reward miners earn for each block is cut in half roughly every four years, an event tied to a fixed block count of 210,000 and commonly called a halving. This stands in deliberate contrast to fiat currencies, whose supply a central bank can expand at its own discretion. Bitcoin also uses what is called the UTXO model, short for unspent transaction output, where a transaction consumes specific prior outputs as inputs and creates new outputs, rather than simply updating an account balance the way Ethereum's account based model does, a structural difference that reflects Bitcoin's narrower focus on transferring discrete units of value rather than maintaining general purpose state.
